transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-14
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Leo Kim (Redwood Solutions) -- Maya Torres (Nebula Head of ML), Ravi Patel (Eng Mgr), Ellen Zhou (SRE), Tom Mendoza (Data Scientist)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC check-in. Reviewed week-over-week token economics (tokens / sec / $), observed caching savings when using prefix/KV cache on chat use-case, discussed batching tradeoffs for latency-sensitive paths, planned more focused KV-prefetch runs and a short benchmark against dedicated instance shapes. Agreed next steps and access items.

Topics discussed:
- Current pilot ingest & traffic shape (bursts, median convo length)
- Observed tokens/sec/$ and how batching + kv/prefix caching shifted cost
- Cache hit patterns and staleness for session-based chats
- Batching windows vs P95 latency targets
- Dedicated vs hosted economics and autoscaling burst behavior
- Action items: perf experiments, access, and pricing sheet

Notes / highlights (auto sections may be imperfect):
- Maya: "We saw last week's burst on Tuesday, like 10x baseline for 6 minutes, that's what spiked our spend"
- Priya: "On our side we enabled prefix cache and saw ~24% token reduction on average for typical multi-turn flows"
- Ravi: "Is that across all models or just the 13b variant?"
- Priya: "Mostly on the 13B-opt family we onboarded; on the larger 70b-ish models the kernel-level quantization helped but network was bigger factor"

Transcript (timestamps approximate):
[00:00] Jordan: ok everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick econ + tuning sync for the nebula pilot. Priya and I will share the perf and we'll get your notes. Maya, do you want to kick off with any updates?
[00:12] Maya: sure, thanks. Um, quick context — the prod-ish load we sent this week was closer to real user mix, so more short chats than earlier. We had a big burst tuesday morning, a bot update caused a rally. That resulted in a big token spike so cost blipped.
[00:29] Ravi: and that was mostly short messages but many concurrent sessions, so tokens/sec went up even if per-session length was smaller.
[00:40] Priya: got it. We looked at the traffic you shared; median conv len is about 5 turns, median tokens per reply ~48, but the inter-arrival has a heavy tail. That tail kills batching efficiency unless you do micro-batches with a fast window.
[00:59] Tom: quick question — when you say caching savings, are you deduping or KV? How is that being counted?
[01:07] Priya: good point — we instrumented both prefix cache and KV cache. Prefix means repeated leading system/prompt tokens we can short-circuit. KV is key-value cache for cached latent states; for our flows prefix caching was the dominant saver because users repeat system prompt and some boilerplate. kv cache helped on longer context continuations, less on single-turn Q/A.
[01:33] Maya: what's the percent saving?
[01:35] Priya: baseline we measured: no cache + default batching = 1.0x cost. With prefix cache we saw ~18-28% token output reduction depending on prompt reuse, and effective tokens/sec/$ improved ~22% in the 13B variant. For multi-turn sessions with high reuse it spiked to 35% savings.
[01:58] Jordan: note there is noise from runtime quantization and kernel selection - the same model shape on a different instance type had different tokens/sec/$. We included standard deviation in the spreadsheet. I'll share that.
[02:10] Ellen: on the SRE side we worry about cache staleness. If users have dynamic system prompts we can't just cache forever. Is there TTL or guardrails?
[02:21] Priya: yes, TTLs and validation. We recommend a session-level key strategy: short TTL (30-120s) for conversational sessions, longer for static prefixes. Also we do conditional invalidation on detected prompt edits. We can share the config we used for the runs.
[02:39] Ravi: about batching: at what window do you see diminishing returns? We can't afford P95 to jump beyond 400ms for some flows.
[02:48] Priya: from our tests, a 20-40ms batch window gives the best tokens/sec/$ while P95 latency impact is minimal for small responses. Past 80ms you start seeing P95 creep. So for latency-sensitive endpoints use micro-batches (20-30ms) and for bulk/async use bigger windows.
[03:05] Tom: are those numbers for hosted or dedicated infra?
[03:08] Priya: those runs were on hosted with our optimized runtime. Dedicated machines with larger GPU memory and better I/O had slightly improved batching efficiency — about 10% better tokens/sec/$. But the headline is: dedicated has better steady throughput and less variance; hosted gives better burst absorbtion without reserved capacity.
[03:29] Maya: curious about CPU overhead too — does batching increase CPU while waiting? Could that push up infra costs?
[03:35] Leo: small amount on orchestration, but main driver is GPU utilization. Batching increases GPU efficiency which lowers per-token GPU cost; orchestrator overhead is marginal compared to that saving.
[03:46] Jordan: to make this practical, we compared three configs you requested: A) hosted default (no custom cache) B) hosted + prefix cache + 30ms batching C) dedicated + prefix + KV prefetch + 40ms batching. The spreadsheet has tokens/sec/$ for each and a projected monthly spend for your traffic shape.
[04:05] Maya: we eyeballed that earlier, C reduced unit cost by about 28% vs A but needs a 3-month reserved window to hit the price — correct?
[04:12] Jordan: roughly yes. Dedicated has commitment-based discounts. We modeled a 3-month and 12-month commit; 12-month has best unit economics but obviously is a contract decision.
[04:22] Ravi: about KV prefetch — that's the one where you prewarm the KV cache for long-running sessions, right? We got weird memory pressure when we tried naive prefetch.
[04:31] Priya: correct. Prefetch can increase memory usage — you need eviction policy tuned. For your workload we recommended LRU with soft limits; in our runs we saw memory bump but within the dedicated shape we recommended it's okay. On hosted we throttle prefetch concurrency.
[04:46] Tom: can we run an experiment where we only prefetch for sessions over X seconds, say > 60s?
[04:50] Priya: yes that's what we planned as next run — we will run two prefetch policies: aggressive (prefetch all sessions after first turn) and conditional (>60s). We'll report results.
[04:58] Maya: also want a run with slightly different prompt templating — we think our UI added a suffix that prevents prefix hit sometimes.
[05:04] Priya: noted. If you can mark canonical templates Tom can sanitize and we'll run with those.
[05:10] Jordan: on the tooling side, we'll give you a perf dashboard link and a short walkthrough. Ellen, you'll get read-only metrics access; can you confirm the right email?
[05:19] Ellen: yes it's ellen.z@nebulasytems.com. I'll add a service account if needed.
[05:24] Jordan: perfect. Two more things — we noticed a small regression in tokens/sec/$ when you switch to the 70B model transiently. That looks like kernel selection fallback where the runtime chose a non-quantized path; we can force a quantized runtime variant if you want to preserve cost.
[05:44] Tom: does forcing quantization change output style? We've seen slight hallucination changes when forcing different kernels before.
[05:49] Priya: sometimes there are minor differences in sampling, but we couple that with eval prompts and a small quality threshold in the optimizer to alert if quality drops beyond your tolerance.
[05:59] Maya: what about security questions — we need SOC2 docs and a note on KMS integration.
[06:04] Jordan: yes, I'll attach the security packet and a short one-pager on KMS/HSM integration. Also note private deployment option (VPC) if you need it; that requires more onboarding time.
[06:17] Ravi: timeline — if we get the 72-hour trace to you Monday, how fast can Redwood run the conditioned prefetch + batching tests?
[06:24] Priya: we can spin up a dedicated bench run in 48 hours given access; results in 72 hours after that. So total ~5 days from trace.
[06:33] Maya: good. Let's go ahead with that.
[06:36] Jordan: recap — Priya will run two prefetch policies + adjusted batching windows against your canonical prompts; Priya to share config + perf sheet by Wed (2026-03-18). Maya/Tom to provide canonical prompt set and 72-hour trace by Fri (2026-03-20). Jordan to send pricing delta + security docs by Thu (2026-03-19). Ellen to provide read-only metrics access by Tue (2026-03-16).
[06:58] Ravi: thanks, that sounds good.
[07:00] Jordan: cool, we'll follow up in email and bump the jira with action items. Thanks everyone.
[07:06] (meeting ends)
